Japan is introducing stricter requirements for foreign nationals seeking permanent residency, including a Japanese language proficiency standard of B1 or higher and an assessment of applicants’ understanding of the country’s laws, rules and social systems. As reported by the Economic Times on Friday, under the proposed framework, most applicants will be expected to demonstrate Japanese language skills equivalent to B1 level under the Reference Framework for Japanese Language Education, published by Japan’s Council for Cultural Affairs on October 12, 2021. The requirement is intended to encourage foreign residents to integrate into Japanese society, communicate effectively, and manage everyday interactions within their communities. However, five categories of applicants will be exempt from the standard language requirement. They include highly skilled foreign professionals covered by specific classifications under Japan’s residence framework, qualifying family members of highly skilled professionals, and foreign nationals who have completed at least six cumulative years of primary or secondary education under Japan’s School Education Act. Children born in Japan whose parent responsible for raising them has Japanese proficiency at B1 level or above will also qualify for an exemption. The fifth category covers applicants granted individual exemptions by the Immigration Services Agency where applying the language requirement is considered unnecessary or inappropriate. The assessment will draw on the government’s Living and Working Guidebook, which provides foreign residents with information about living and working in the country. Applicants who demonstrate limited understanding of these rules or show little willingness to learn about them could receive an unfavourable assessment. The Commissioner of the Immigration Services Agency will determine the procedures for conducting this assessment. The seven categories are: Spouses of Japanese citizens. Children of Japanese citizens. Spouses of permanent residents. Children of permanent residents. Spouses of special permanent residents. Children of special permanent residents. Individuals recognised as requiring international protection by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) or another recognised international organisation. For individuals recognised under international protection frameworks, the financial self-sufficiency requirement may be waived, subject to additional conditions established by the Ministry of Justice. Applicants in the other categories are generally still expected to demonstrate financial independence. Exemptions do not guarantee approval Despite the relaxed conditions available to certain groups, eligibility does not automatically translate into permanent residency approval. Applicants must generally demonstrate good conduct, comply with Japanese laws and fulfil their financial obligations, including paying taxes and other public charges. The Minister of Justice retains final authority to decide whether granting permanent residency serves Japan’s national interest. The changes underline Japan’s emphasis on language ability, social integration, and compliance with national rules in its permanent residency assessment process.
